title: Identification of a universal three-body s-wave resonance in ^10He

paper_content.abstract:
Universality in physics describes the emergence of common features in vastly
different systems. One fascinating example is the Efimov phenomenon where
three-body resonantly interacting systems display universal properties. Efimov
states have been observed in ultra-cold-atom systems, but their manifestation
in nuclei remains elusive due to the long-range repulsive Coulomb interaction
and the stringent requirement for at least two s-wave resonances in its subsys-
tems. Recent theories propose another universality in three-body halos with only
one s-wave resonance. Here, we report the identification of a precursor of this
phenomenon in a neutron-rich 10He nucleus. With higher statistics and better
sensitivities than previous experiments, we identify two low-lying 0+ states of
10He at 1 MeV and 2 MeV above its two-neutron decay threshold, and deter-
mine an s-wave scattering length of 3.5 fm between 8He and neutron. It is
revealed that the lower energy state, the ground state of 10He, is a three-body
state with only s-wave interactions among its subsystems. This state manifests
as a resonance structure, which is a direct consequence of a universal long-range
three-body repulsion. Our work sheds new light on quantum halos with finite life-
times, providing a path toward their unified understanding across various scales
and fields.
paper_content.introduction:
In few-body quantum systems with short-range interactions and large s-wave scatter-
ing lengths (a ) relative to the interaction range, universal low-energy phenomena can
emerge [1, 2]. One of the most prominent examples is the universality found by Efimov
that there are infinite series of three-body bound states with universal energy and spa-
tial structures when the inter-particle scattering length a is infinitely large [3–5]. The
phenomena in atomic and molecular systems governed by the electromagnetic inter-
actions have been extensively investigated with cold atoms (see ref. [6] and references
therein). Alternatively, in the world of nuclei dominated by the strong interaction,
nuclei around the neutron drip line are also expected to provide excellent opportunities
to search for such phenomena (see ref. [5] and references therein).

A key aspect underlying the few-body universality is the emergence of a long-range
three-body force induced by multiple s-wave scatterings [7]. For the Efimov state,
an attractive three-body force is created from the two-body subsystems which are
marginally bound or unbound. Such a halo state can mediate attractive force between
the other particles up to a substantially large distance, forming the Efimov bound
states. It has also been predicted that the Efimov’s universal three-body effect can
extend to resonant states [8] and virtual states [9]. Recently, it has been shown that
universal geometric properties for three-body nuclear halo states may also appear when
the s-wave interactions in part of the two-body subsystems are not resonant [10, 11].
Distinct from the Efimov states, the universal halo states originate from a long-range
repulsion and have not been observed experimentally in any atomic or nuclear systems
to date. In the present work, we examine the low-energy properties and the related
three-body effects in an unbound system in nuclear physics: the helium-10 (10He)
nucleus, consisting of a 8He core and two valence neutrons.

The nature of the 10He ground state has been the focus of keen debate since
its discovery in RIKEN in 1994 [12]. Up to now, two contradictory results exist for
the ground state energy of 10He. The 8He-n-n relative energy (E ) spectra from
the 11Li(-p) [12–14] and 14Be(-2p2n) [15] knockout reactions show a prominent low-
lying peak at 1.5(1) MeV (the weighted average of 1.2(3) MeV [12], 1.7(4) MeV [13],
1.54(11) MeV [14], and 1.60(25) MeV [15]) with a width Γ of 1-2 MeV. The 11Li(d,
3He) reaction shows a ground-state peak at 1.4(3) MeV (Γ 1.5 MeV) [16]. However,
the 3H(8He,p)10He two-neutron (2n) transfer reaction reported a higher ground-state
energy at 2.1(2) MeV (Γ 2 MeV) [17]. Currently, the most advanced theoretical
work on 10He is given in Refs. [18, 19]. On the one hand, it has been discussed that
the 10He ground state could be at 2 MeV, as observed by the 2n transfer reaction,
and has a [0p ]2 structure, while the initial-state effects due to the halo nature of
11Li or 14Be may lower the energy of 10He to 1.5 MeV as observed in knockout
reactions. Calculations with such effects qualitatively agree with the 10He invariant-
mass spectrum from 11Li(-p) [19] but similar calculations assuming a direct α-particle
removal from 14Be cannot explain the spectrum from 14Be(-α or -2p2n) [20]. On the
other hand, the 8He-n-n three-body model calculations predicted that 10He could have
two low-lying 0+ states with [1s ]2 and [0p ]2 valence neutron structures [18, 21],
that are built on the 1/2+ (8He ν1s ) or 1/2 (8He ν0p ) states of
9He. The observed 10He ground-state energy variation thus could be caused by two
overlapping 0+ states populated with different strengths in knockout and transfer
reactions [18, 22]. The [1s ]2 component, that is characterized as a three-body s-
wave resonance built from the s-wave virtual states in the n-n and 8He-n subsystems,
has not been identified in any experiments so far.

Here, we show the energy spectrum and three-body correlations of 10He measured
using the invariant-mass technique with higher statistics and better sensitivities than
previous experiments. It is concluded that the 10He ground state is a three-body s-
wave resonance, where both the n-n and 8He-n subsystems have zero relative angular
momenta. Such a state shows features that arise from the long-range repulsion and
represents an unbound analogue of the universal halo states predicted by Hongo and
Son [10].
paper_content.results:
The two-neutron unbound 10He was produced through quasi-free knockout (p, 2p)
reaction at 250 MeV/nucleon, using an intense 11Li beam bombarding on the 150-
mm thick liquid hydrogen target of the MINOS device [23]. The 8He fragment and two
neutrons from the 10He decay were detected by the SAMURAI spectrometer [24] and
the neutron detector array NEBULA [25], respectively. The same setup was used in
Refs. [26–30]. Since 8He has no bound excited states, we do not require γ-ray detection
in coincidence.

The three-body relative energy E , which is also the energy of 10He above the
8He + 2n threshold, was reconstructed by the momenta of 8He and the two neutrons.
The typical energy resolution at E = 1 MeV is about σ = 0.15 MeV (see Methods).
To reject the cross-talk background mainly caused by neutron scattering within the
NEBULA detectors, we applied the procedures detailed in Ref. [31] (see Methods).
The overall 2n detection efficiency as a function of E is shown in the upper panel of
Fig. 1, which demonstrates sufficient sensitivity down to the decay threshold.

The lower panel of Fig. 1 shows the relative-energy spectrum after the efficiency
correction, which has much smaller statistical uncertainties compared to two pre-
vious experiments at 61 MeV/nucleon at RIKEN [12] and at 280 MeV/nucleon
at Gesellschaft fu¨r Schwerionenforschung (GSI) [14]. The present spectrum of 10He
shows a low-energy peak at E 1.5 MeV, consistent with the previous results in
Refs [12, 14]. In Refs. [12, 14], the peak at 1.5 MeV has been interpreted as the
ground state of 10He. In addition to this low-energy peak, the current data clearly
show a shoulder structure below 1 MeV, that was unresolved in the spectrum mea-
sured previously at RIKEN but was missing in the GSI result. The difference at small
relative energies has been reported before in the study of 11Li [32] and 6He [33], which
was attributed to the enhanced experimental sensitivity at low relative energies in the
current setup. The low-lying shoulder indicates that the peak at 1.5 MeV is not
the ground state of 10He. Above 2 MeV, the current data, with much better quality,
exhibit strength extending to higher excitation energies.

Here, we compare the data to theoretical calculations that combine the coupled-
channel 9Li + n + n three-body model of 11Li and the quasi-free knockout (p, pN)
reaction model. The three-body model reproduces well the ground-state properties of
the 11Li nucleus, including the 2n separation energy, matter and charge radii. The
dominant 2n configurations with a 9Li core are 47% [0p ]2 and a large s-wave mix-
ing of 44% [1s ]2 that generates the neutron halo structure and strong dineutron
correlations. The neutron configurations are in reasonable agreement with the recent
results from the 11Li(p, pn) reaction [27]. In the calculation, a 0p -orbital proton
is removed from the 9Li core, resulting in the population of the 8He ground state
that has a [0s ]2[0p ]4 neutron shell structure. The p-wave proton removal has
been confirmed by comparing the experimental momentum distributions of 10He to
the quasi-free knockout calculations (see Methods). The final 10He states were com-
puted with the complex-scaled solutions of Lippmann-Schwinger equation (CSLS)
method [34, 35], which is a suitable approach to describe three-body scattering states
including virtual states, and to investigate their decay mechanisms. We adopted the
8He-n folding potential and the realistic Argonne v8 force for the n-n potential [36].
Considering the uncertainty of the 8He-n interaction (see for instance a compilation
of resonances in 9He in ref. [37]), we allow variations in the parameters governing this
interaction. See Methods for details.

The calculated E distributions are shown in Fig. 1, which have been convo-
luted with the experimental resolution detailed in Methods. The calculation results
for the 8He-n subsystem, with the tuned 8He-n interaction to fit the current 10He
spectrum below 2 MeV, produced an s-wave scattering length between 8He and neu-
tron (a ) of 3.5 fm, in reasonable agreement with the results from some knockout
reactions ( 3.17(66) fm [14], 3 fm < a < 0 fm [38], 2.1(6) fm or 6.8(14) fm [39])
and the weak 8He-n s-wave attraction from the (p,p) resonance elastic scattering [40],
but not with the strong one (a 10 fm) reported in Ref. [41] and Ref. [42]. A
recent analysis of the (p, p) resonance elastic scattering data with more advanced
treatment of the isospin symmetry also suggests a small negative a [43]. In addi-
tion, the current calculations produce a broad p-wave resonance for 9He at 0.76 MeV
(Γ = 0.95 MeV), in reasonable agreement with the extracted 8He-n relative energy
spectrum from the present experiment [44].

To pin down the origin of the low-energy peak, we decomposed the E spectrum
into contributions from different decay channels in the final scattering states. It is
shown in Fig. 1 that the low-lying shoulder structure is dominated by the 8He +
[1s ]2 component, peaked at 0.96 MeV, while the peak at around 1.5 MeV in the
spectrum is due to the mixture of the 8He + [1s ]2 and 8He + [0p ]2
components. The 8He + [0p ]2 component gives a broad 10He resonance peaked
at 1.9 MeV, consistent with the 10He 0+ state reported by the 2n transfer reaction [17],
but with a smaller decay width (Γ 1.6 MeV). This finding resolves the long-standing
puzzle about the different 10He ground-state energies obtained from knockout and
2n transfer reactions. Our work suggests that the ground state of 10He has a nearly
pure [s]2 configuration. The 10He, which is traditionally considered as a doubly magic
nucleus, thus appears as a “double-intruder” nucleus with the last two neutrons mainly
in the 1s shell, in line with the intruder s-wave dominated ground state of 9He. The
intruder dominant configuration could be understood in the shell-model framework
due to the melting of the N=8 shell closure for the neutron-rich isotopes below Z=4.
In addition, the cross-section ratio for populating the excited 0+ state relative to the
ground state was extracted to be about 0.36. This value is in contrast to the estimation
of a simple direct-reaction model presented in Ref. [22], where a pure [sd]2-dominant
configuration in the ground state of 10He was expected to yield a ratio greater than
1.5.

Our theoretical calculations reproduce the data below E = 2 MeV, nevertheless,
they underestimate the strength at higher excitation energies. The reason might be
due to higher-order transitions or higher-lying states that are not accounted for in the
calculations. Indeed, existence of 2+ state with resonance energies around 4-6 MeV [14–
16, 45], 1 state near 5.5 MeV [17] and 3 state around 7.9 MeV [45] have been
suggested. Incorporation of these states into the fitting improves the agreement with
the E spectrum in the higher energy region, but it has minimal impact on the fit
results below 2 MeV. In our calculations, the spectrum’s shape is highly sensitive to
the 8He-n interaction, and the observed low-energy structure is reproduced only with
a weakly attractive 8He-n s-wave interaction. Futhermore, deactivating the final-state
interactions (FSI) results in a shift of the excitation strength towards higher energies,
coinciding with the disappearance of the [0p ]2 resonance and a broadening of the
peak from the [1s ]2 neutrons. See Methods for details. This indicates that the 10He
structure observed in the spectrum below 2 MeV primarily arises from the FSI rather
than the initial-state effects.

The above analyses demonstrate that the lowest-energy structure in 10He is a three-
body state with zero relative angular momenta (s-wave) among its subsystems. In a
two-body system, such a virtual state with orbital angular momentum L = 0, due to
the absence of centrifugal barrier, can only exist as a threshold peculiarity which can-
not be physically detected as a distinct peak. In contrast, the present case exhibits a
well-defined resonance structure, with positive energy and finite width, which is obvi-
ously different from the threshold peculiarity. Such an s-wave resonance peak appears
only in systems with 3 particles and can be attributed to a non-zero value of the
effective angular momentum K, which characterizes the long-range behaviour of the
three-body potential [2, 11, 18] (see Methods for the definition of K). Indeed, even for
a non-interacting three-body system, the hyperradial (i.e. three-body effective) poten-
tial is repulsive with K =3/2. More precisely, in our system, a large neutron-neutron
s-wave scattering length of a 18.6 fm [47] reduces the effective angular momen-

based on the Faddeev approach). This is physically due to that a neutron occupy-
ing the halo virtual state can mediate an attractive interaction between the other
neutron and the 8He core up to a large distance of a , thereby effectively reduc-
nn

potential retains its repulsive character in the 8He-n-n three-body system. This mech-

effect [3, 7]. While K is imaginary in the Efimov effect, our system shows universal
long-range repulsion with K = 1/2 because of a small core-neutron s-wave scatter-
ing length of a 3.5 fm. Recently, Hongo and Son predicted that weakly bound

structural properties distinct from the Efimov states as a consequence of the universal
long-range repulsion [11]. Observation of the resonance structure for the three-body
s-wave “virtual” state in the 8He-n-n system can be consistently interpreted as aris-
ing from this long-range universal repulsion. Thus, the present work identifies the
ground state 10He as an unbound analogue of the universal 2n halo states [10, 11]. To
further unveil the nature of this novel universal quantum halo, it is pivotal to scruti-
nize their structural properties, with concurrent developments in low-energy nuclear
experiments and theoretical models on the three-body resonances.

In summary, we have reported on the low-lying states in 10He populated from the
11Li(p,2p) knockout reactions at 250 MeV/nucleon. Two low-lying 0+ states of 10He
were identified at about 1 MeV and 2 MeV, which have a [1s ]2
0+
and a [0p ]2
0+
neutron configuration, respectively, clarifying the long-standing puzzle about the dif-
ferent 10He ground-state energies obtained from knockout and 2n transfer reactions.
An s-wave scattering length of 3.5 fm between 8He and neutron was extracted
from the current 10He spectrum. The existence of a three-body s-wave resonance in
10He was conclusively elucidated through the high statistic invariant-mass spectrum
and the correlation analysis among the three decay particles. The three-body effect
analogous to the Efimov physics is presented as the origin for the three-body repulsive
barrier. The ground state of 10He represents an unbound analogue of the universal
three-body halo states. While these phenomena have been observed in a nuclear sys-
tem, we anticipate analogous behavior in other few-body systems, including exotic
hadrons and condensed matter systems, and particularly in ultracold atomic systems,
where tunable s-wave interactions between constituent particles enable systematic
exploration.

Isotope Beam Factory operated by the RIKEN Nishina Center and the Center for
Nuclear Study of the University of Tokyo. Cocktail secondary beam was first produced
through fragmentation of a 345 MeV/nucleon 48Ca primary beam on a 9Be target.
The typical intensity of the primary beam is 400 particle nA. The secondary beam
was then purified and identified event by event using the BigRIPS two-stage fragment
separator [48]. The average energy of the 11Li beam is 246 MeV/nucleon, with a purity

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Referee report for the paper
First identification of a universal three-body s-wave resonance in 10 He
by Y.L. Sun et al
The new highly accurate data on 10He populated in the proton knockout reaction
from 11Li halo nucleus is reported in this work. The Authors report on the
low-energy enhancement in the invariant mass spectrum of 10He, which was not
identified in the previous studies due to insufficient resolution or/and statistics.
These data are interpreted as providing evidence to existence of s-wave
resonance in 10He, built on three attractive s-wave pairwise interactions.
Such a resonance is discussed as representative of the "universal" long-range
dynamics of Efimov type. The search for these class of phenomenon was
was so far unsuccessful in nuclear systems, therefore such a discovery
could be a real "gem" in the studies of exotic phenomena near the nuclear
driplines.
In my analysis of situation I fully rely on the reliability of the data.
These are provided by one of leading groups in the field with broad expertise
in analogous studies. So, in the following analysis of the proposed
interpretation complete reliability of the data is implied.
There are important questions about interpretation of the data. It can be
found in the literature that alternative interpretations are possible.
These interpretations are for a long time "on the market" and should
not be neglected without significant explanation.
It should be noted that alternative interpretations are also not trivial
and are related to questionable types of the long-range dynamics in
nuclear systems, which are also of significant interest.
I find the experimental observations of this paper and various types of
associated physical phenomena sufficiently interesting to be published in Nature.
However, major revision of the manuscript in aspects concerning the
data interpretation is due (see the discussion below).
I would strongly recommend this paper for publication in Nature if my
criticism concerning interpretation is fully taken into account.
=========================================================================
Point 1. Scattering length in the 9He=8He+n.
Broad theoretical exploratory studies of the 10He spectra sensitivity to the
s-wave 8He-n interaction have been performed in Ref. [18] by Grigorenko and Zhukov.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Since further we rely on the results of Refs. [18, 19], it is necessary
to comment to their description in this work:
"Currently, the most advanced theoretical work on 10He is given in
Refs. [18, 19]. On the one hand, it has been discussed that the
10He ground state could be at ∼ 2 MeV, as observed by the 2n
transfer reaction, and has a [0p_1/2]^2_{0+} structure, while
the initial state effects due to the halo nature of 11Li or
14Be may lower the energy of 10He to ∼1.5 MeV as observed in
knockout reactions. Calculations with such effects qualitatively
agree with the 10He invariant-mass spectrum from 11Li(-p) [19]
but cannot explain the spectrum from 14Be(-2p2n) [20]."
(1) The low energy strength in the 10He spectrum has mixed character
[0s_1/2]^2_{0+} + [0p_1/2]^2_{0+} with around 50% mixing. Important
special attention was paid in [18] to evolution of these components
in various conditions.
(2) The statement that the results if [19] "cannot explain the
spectrum from 14Be(-2p2n)" is not relevant, since the calculations
in [19] were about alpha knockout, while there were no clear identification
of the reaction channel in [20] and "14Be(-2p2n)" (not alpha removal!) is
just one of reasonable assumptions of this work.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Let's have a look
in Fig. 5f of this work. The solid curve shows the spectrum which is very
consistent with the new experimental data. In Fig. 6c the decomposition
of exactly this spectrum is shown demonstrating energy split between [s^2]_0 and
[p^2]_0 components at about 1 MeV, which is, again, very consistent with
theoretical results shown in Fig. 1 of this work. The complete three-body
correlations for this case also can be found in Fig. 13c of Ref. [18]. These
are calculated not exactly for the excitation energy range, used in Fig. 2
of the Refereed paper, but they looks very similar to the recent data.
So, the agreement of this specific theoretical prediction with the data seem
to be very good. However, this specific calculation corresponds to quite a
different scattering length 2.9 fm in the 8He+n, which is not ATTRACTIVE,
but REPULSIVE. This is not in accord about the basic message of this work
about universal Efimov-type phenomenon.
Let's have a look on the situation in a different way. The energy of the
p_{1/2} resonant state used in the calculations of this work is mentioned
to be 0.76 MeV. The results for such p_{1/2} position can be found in
Fig. 5d of [18]. They should be between dotted and dash-dotted curve,
producing peak between 30 and 200 keV. So, there seem to be strong
contradiction between theoretical approaches of this work and of Ref.
[18]. According to [18] the universal s-wave structure built on the
s-wave attractions in all three subsystems should have been seen as
extreme low-energy (100 keV? 200 keV?) structure in this reaction.
I would mention one qualitatively suspicious moment in the provided theoretical
calculations. Based on the energy of p_{1/2} state 0.76 MeV, the trivial
independent particle approximation should provide the energy ∼1.5 MeV
for the [p_{1/2}^2]_0 configuration. The peak energy for this configuration in
Fig. 1 of this work is ∼1.9 MeV. This means that the paring interaction
is effectively repulsive for the [p_{1/2}^2]_0 configuration. This is quite
unexpected result, which I see as strange for the three-body model and which
it is not within the systematics of effective pairing energies for the
p_{1/2} subshell, which can be traced for the other members of N=8
isotone. In Ref. [18] these effective pairing energies vary from 0.5 to 1.8 MeV,
which is smaller then the typical values in the p_{3/2} subshell, but
not negative at least.
The strong theoretical controversy is quite intriguing, considering the
nice agreement between the three-body calculations of this group [33] and
[Grigorenko et al. PRC 102, 014611 (2020)] for another quite complicated
peripheral phenomenon: soft dipole excitation in the continuum of 6He system.
It is not impossible that quite old calculations of Ref. [18] are deficient
in some way. However, unless this deficiency is demonstrated they can not
be just disregarded: these are published and well documented results, while
for the calculations of this work not much details are available. The Authors
should either find out what is wrong with calculations of [18] or rely on
them as alternative interpretation of the data.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Some separate note concerning the 8He+n scattering length issue.
I would like to pay attention of the Authors to results of paper
[Khirk et al., Phys. Rev. C 111, L051601 (2025)].
In this work the data of Uberseder et al. [39] were reinterpreted with more advanced
treatment of isospin symmetry. The scattering length in the 8He+n channel
deduced in this work was weakly attractive as -2.7 fm, with no need for s_{1/2}
resonance. This is quite close to the deduced in this work value −3.45 fm.
However, the p_{1/2} state should be at about 2.3 MeV (original
analysis of Uberseder et al. do not allow any resonances with l>0 and
E<3 MeV at all).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
=========================================================================
Point 2. Reaction mechanism issue.
The structures promoted in this paper as "two low-lying 0+ states of 10He
at ∼1 MeV and ∼2 MeV above its two-neutron decay threshold" according to
calculations of [18] are strongly sensitive to the reaction mechanism.
Let's compare solid curves Fig. 5 c and f in [18]. One is well consistent
with the data of the refereed work the other is shifted to higher energy
to more than 1 MeV. The same if we compare Fig. 6 b and c in [18]. For
one the [s^2]_0 and [p^2]_0 components are well energy split (as in the
calculations of this work), but for the
other they more or less overlaps, so we can hardly speculate about
separate [s^2]_0 and [p^2]_0 states.
The results of the refereed work are based on some realistic reaction model
where the 11Li WF is present. So, all these effects should be there, they
are just not discussed. These could be easily checked if I am right
by the Authors of this work in two reasonably simple ways:
(1) By performing calculations without 10He FSI - just plane waves.
Typically people try to check, whether the signal they see is not provided
just by a plane wave, without any dynamics.
(2) By changing the reaction mechanism by using not a halo nucleus 11Li,
but a compact system. For example 14C(-4p). Not very realistic reaction
for practical realization, but theoretically we may play games. If the
strength function is strongly qualitatively sensitive to the reaction
mechanism, then you can hardly speculate about resonance states. Resonant
states is something independent on reaction mechanism by definition.
Also, if your population cross section strongly depends on the reaction
mechanism then what is your "universality" about? This is not about that the
story is not interesting and important, but about carefully choosing terms
for the discussion.
I am a bit amused that this topic is total missing in the manuscript,
since the Authors has recently studies soft dipole excitation in 6He [33],
where they do not attempt to interpret the E1 strength function in terms
of resonance position and width.
=========================================================================
Point 3. Possibility of 1- state population.
The excitations of 10He with J>0 are only briefly discussed in this work
as possibly contributing the high-energy part of the strength function.
This is not substantiated with any calculations. However, it was shown
in [19] that due to extreme halo extent of the 11Li WF the specific mechanism of
proton knockout may lead to population of 1- as the lowest energy
component of the 10He spectrum. It should be noted that mechanism of
such a knockout is not just s-wave removal
and do not lead to typical s-wave momentum distributions
of the spectator in the outgoing channel (see Fig. 2 of [19]).
The population of the 1- configuration was predicted on the level up to
25% to the 0+ population rate. However, the low-energy region, where
a specific enhancement was observed in the 11Li(-p) reaction, the
1- may provide dominating contribution.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Please check the following:
Text:
"As shown in Fig.4, the distributions can be well reproduced by the quasi
free knockout calculations that assume a p-wave proton removal from 11Li."
Caption Fig.4:
"s-wave (red solid line) or p-wave (blue solid line)"
There is agreement with the red solid line in the figure, which is in
contradiction with the text.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
=========================================================================
Minor things
I find the presentation of data of [Korsheninnikov et al] misleading in Fig. 1.
The original paper contains the data on CD_2 and C targets, which are not in
full agreement. The conclusions of [Korsheninnikov et al] are based on subtracted,
spectrum which has large error bars, while the authors of this work arbitrarily
have chosen one of initial spectra with comfortably small error bars.
I sincerely believe that considering all the problematic issues discussed above
the deduced scattering length precision "−3.45(20) fm" is a strong overestimation
of the achievable precision. Something like "∼ -3.5 fm" will be more realistic,
since criterion of the error determination is unclear.
The Authors use two Figures (2 and 3) to show the complete three-body correlation
patterns and their projections. I think it could be more instructive to demonstrate
evolution of the correlation patterns with energy. According to the theoretical
interpretation there are energy ranges where the [s^2]_0 component is totally
dominant and where the [p^2]_0 contribution is important. It is a bit strange
not to try to observe the difference in the correlations.
The same is somehow true about Fig. 4. When gated on the excitations of 10He
these spectra may (or may not) demonstrate some differences related to
peculiarities of reaction mechanisms populating [s^2]_0 and [p^2]_0 configurations
(if there are any).
I find the topic "Deduction of the effective angular momentum for a
three-body system". On one hand, the relevance of this derivation to the topic
of the paper is doubtful. On the other hand, this derivation is valid within the
specific adiabatic framework. The conclusion of this derivation is trivial:
between "no s-wave interaction" and "Efimov case" there will be a continuum
of effective interactions as the pairwise scattering lengths (all together
simultaneously or in some separate manner) tend from zero to minus infinity.
Do not think this deserve publication in the Nature.
===========================================================================
To finalize the discussion. All the theoretical points above are quite complicated.
I doubt that within the limited volume this particular publication the
mentioned controversies could be well resolved.
However, these theoretical discussions also do not devaluate the potential importance of
the current experimental observation and its interest to a broad scientific community.
My proposal is to reformulate the paper from modality "solidly understood in a unique way"
(which I doubt the Authors can actually prove) to "there are different possible
intriguing interpretations of the data". Possible alternative interpretations should
be clearly discussed in the paper. They are also not trivial and may be of significant
scientific interest by themselves as ideas existing in parallel with ideology of
Efimov-type phenomena. The title of the paper should be also changed to a broader
context and statements about "resonant states" replaced everywhere with something
neutral like "peaks in the population cross section".
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Report on "First identification of a universal three-body s-wave resonance in $^{10}$He"
The subject of this paper is the experimental identification of an Efimov state (resonance) in the $^{10}$He system.
Although Efimov states were first observed in cold atom systems and have long
been discussed in the context of atomic He$_{3}$, they were originally predicted
within the realm of nuclear physics by Efimov. I believe it is extremely
important to identify nuclear systems that can be described by this universal
model, further highlighting the universality of Efimov physics. For this reason,
I think the present paper, especially given its experimental nature, deserves
publication.
I have only a few remarks, which do not pertain to the experimental techniques
that are well explained.
1. A simple remark is on line 6, where the emergence of an infinite tower of
three-body states is related, strictly speaking, to an infinite (and not just a
sufficiently large) scattering length.
2. The explanation of the resonance is mostly based on the shell model
interpretation of the state. It would be useful for a reader from another
community (thanks to the universality of Efimov physics) to at least provide a
sketch of what is happening and why the state appears as a double-intruder
nucleus (lines 45-..., 90-..., and 122).
3. The explanation of the state rests heavily on the shell model. However, there
are other ways to view it that rely on both the scattering length, which has
been extracted (as mentioned again in line 199), and on the effective range
(Kievsky A., Gattobigio M., Girlanda L., Viviani M., *Efimov Physics and
Connections to Nuclear Physics.*, Annu. Rev. Nucl. Part. Sci **71**, 465,
2021). It would be important to try to extract the effective range to allow
for other interpretations of the same state.
4. The grand-angular momentum K is discussed in the Methods section, but I'm not
sure that the introduction of K in line 171 without a previous explanation is
correct.
To summarize, the paper deserves publication as it sheds a nuclear
light on Efimov physics, which originates from Nuclear Physics.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Summary
The manuscript describes measurements of 10He produced through (p, 2p) reactions of a ∼250 MeV/u 11Li beam with a
liquid hydrogen target. Analysis of the three-body relative energy and Jacobi correlation spectra utilized a coupled-channel
three-body model of 11Li combined with the quasi-free knockout reaction model, and complex-scaled solutions of the
Lippmann-Schwinger equation were used to compute final states in 10He. The low-energy structure in the three-body
relative energy spectrum is explained by two 0+ states with 8He cores, one with a [1s1/2]2 neutron component and another
with a [0p1/2]2 neutron component. By tuning the 8He-n interaction to fit the 10He spectrum below 2 MeV, the authors
extracted an s-wave scattering length between 8He and the neutron. The Jacobi-T normalized relative energy and Jacobi-Y
angle 8He-n-n correlations gated on relative energies < 1 MeV show enhancements that are qualitatively reproduced by the
three-body calculations. The authors conclude that the observation of the two 0+ states resolves the long-standing difference
between 10He ground state energies measured from knockout and 2n transfer. Furthermore, the 10He ground state is a
three-body s-wave resonance that exemplifies a novel class of universal three-body bound states.
Revisions
The paper is well-constructed, concise, and it provides new information suggesting a resolution to a long-standing question
about the structure of 10He. The following revisions would strengthen the paper and should be satisfactorily addressed:
1. How is the 1-sigma energy resolution dependence as a function of relative energy determined? Does this come from a
previous measurement? A Monte Carlo simulation of the setup? A brief explanation or reference in Section 2 is necessary to
support the stated relationship. An addition to the top panel in Fig. 1 to show the resolution alongside the efficiency or an
illustration and accompanying explanation in the methods section would help further convince the reader of the setup’s
sensitivity.
2. Including additional information in the Methods section about the cross-talk rejection procedures would benefit the reader.
For example, reference [31] includes empirically derived values for the same-wall cross-talk rejection filters based on the
7Li(p,n)7Be test case. Are similar values used here?
3. Some clarification of the analysis procedure is needed to help the reader understand the comparison between data and
calculation shown in Fig. 1.
a. How does the output from the three-body 11Li model + quasi-free knockout model inform the calculation of the final 10He
states? Do the reaction calculations provide cross-sections that scale the contributions of the 10He states in the relative
energy spectrum?
b. What parameters for the 8He-n interaction are varied and how? Including an additional figure in the Methods section that
shows how these parameters impact the agreement with data would help reinforce the assertion from lines 131 – 133: “the
spectrum’s shape is highly sensitive to the 8He-n interaction, and the observed low-energy structure is reproduced only with
a weakly attractive 8He-n s-wave interaction.”
4. The legend and caption for Fig. 1 should be revised to clarify what is indicated by the green dashed curve labeled ‘others.’
It’s not clear if this is referring to the discussion in lines 124 – 131 regarding higher-lying states.
5. Does the Argonne v8’ force include/account for the large neutron-neutron s-wave scattering length ann ∼ 19 fm referenced
in line 174?
6. Is it possible to extract cross-sections for populating the two 0+ states? Or a ratio of these cross-sections? This could be
useful for comparing to previous predictions e.g. reference [22].
7. The [2s1/2]2 should be [1s1/2]2 to be consistent with notation elsewhere (e.g. the legend of Fig. 1 and line 196).
8. In lines 173-174 and in the Methods section, the 10He ground state is shown to have an effective angular momentum
K=1/2 which should be associated with a repulsive effective three-body potential indicated by the black curve in Fig. 5. The
next line seems contradictory: “This is physically due to that a neutron occupying the halo virtual state can mediate an
attractive interaction between the other neutron and the 8He core up to large distance …” And line 180 emphasizes again
the 10He system shows long-range repulsion. The explanation of how the attractive interaction arises needs to be clarified.
9. In the methods subsection “deduction of the effective angular momentum for a three-body system,” additional context is
needed around line 304 to explain or justify why the right hand side of Eq.(6) is O(1) so that the leading order term of the left-
hand side must vanish.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Universality in physics describes the emergence of common features in vastly
different systems. One fascinating example is the Efimov phenomenon where
three-body resonantly interacting systems display universal properties. Efimov
states have been observed in ultra-cold-atom systems, but their manifestation
in nuclei remains elusive due to the long-range repulsive Coulomb interaction
and the stringent requirement for at least two s-wave resonances in its subsys-
tems. Recent theories propose another universality in three-body halos with only
one s-wave resonance. Here, we report the identification of a precursor of this
phenomenon in a neutron-rich 10He nucleus. With higher statistics and better
sensitivities than previous experiments, we identify two low-lying 0+ states of
10He at 1 MeV and 2 MeV above its two-neutron decay threshold, and deter-
mine an s-wave scattering length of 3.5 fm between 8He and neutron. It is
revealed that the lower energy state, the ground state of 10He, is a three-body
state with only s-wave interactions among its subsystems. This state manifests
as a resonance structure, which is a direct consequence of a universal long-range
three-body repulsion. Our work sheds new light on quantum halos with finite life-
times, providing a path toward their unified understanding across various scales
and fields.

---

## Introduction

In few-body quantum systems with short-range interactions and large s-wave scatter-
ing lengths (a ) relative to the interaction range, universal low-energy phenomena can
emerge [1, 2]. One of the most prominent examples is the universality found by Efimov
that there are infinite series of three-body bound states with universal energy and spa-
tial structures when the inter-particle scattering length a is infinitely large [3–5]. The
phenomena in atomic and molecular systems governed by the electromagnetic inter-
actions have been extensively investigated with cold atoms (see ref. [6] and references
therein). Alternatively, in the world of nuclei dominated by the strong interaction,
nuclei around the neutron drip line are also expected to provide excellent opportunities
to search for such phenomena (see ref. [5] and references therein).

A key aspect underlying the few-body universality is the emergence of a long-range
three-body force induced by multiple s-wave scatterings [7]. For the Efimov state,
an attractive three-body force is created from the two-body subsystems which are
marginally bound or unbound. Such a halo state can mediate attractive force between
the other particles up to a substantially large distance, forming the Efimov bound
states. It has also been predicted that the Efimov’s universal three-body effect can
extend to resonant states [8] and virtual states [9]. Recently, it has been shown that
universal geometric properties for three-body nuclear halo states may also appear when
the s-wave interactions in part of the two-body subsystems are not resonant [10, 11].
Distinct from the Efimov states, the universal halo states originate from a long-range
repulsion and have not been observed experimentally in any atomic or nuclear systems
to date. In the present work, we examine the low-energy properties and the related
three-body effects in an unbound system in nuclear physics: the helium-10 (10He)
nucleus, consisting of a 8He core and two valence neutrons.

The nature of the 10He ground state has been the focus of keen debate since
its discovery in RIKEN in 1994 [12]. Up to now, two contradictory results exist for
the ground state energy of 10He. The 8He-n-n relative energy (E ) spectra from
the 11Li(-p) [12–14] and 14Be(-2p2n) [15] knockout reactions show a prominent low-
lying peak at 1.5(1) MeV (the weighted average of 1.2(3) MeV [12], 1.7(4) MeV [13],
1.54(11) MeV [14], and 1.60(25) MeV [15]) with a width Γ of 1-2 MeV. The 11Li(d,
3He) reaction shows a ground-state peak at 1.4(3) MeV (Γ 1.5 MeV) [16]. However,
the 3H(8He,p)10He two-neutron (2n) transfer reaction reported a higher ground-state
energy at 2.1(2) MeV (Γ 2 MeV) [17]. Currently, the most advanced theoretical
work on 10He is given in Refs. [18, 19]. On the one hand, it has been discussed that
the 10He ground state could be at 2 MeV, as observed by the 2n transfer reaction,
and has a [0p ]2 structure, while the initial-state effects due to the halo nature of
11Li or 14Be may lower the energy of 10He to 1.5 MeV as observed in knockout
reactions. Calculations with such effects qualitatively agree with the 10He invariant-
mass spectrum from 11Li(-p) [19] but similar calculations assuming a direct α-particle
removal from 14Be cannot explain the spectrum from 14Be(-α or -2p2n) [20]. On the
other hand, the 8He-n-n three-body model calculations predicted that 10He could have
two low-lying 0+ states with [1s ]2 and [0p ]2 valence neutron structures [18, 21],
that are built on the 1/2+ (8He ν1s ) or 1/2 (8He ν0p ) states of
9He. The observed 10He ground-state energy variation thus could be caused by two
overlapping 0+ states populated with different strengths in knockout and transfer
reactions [18, 22]. The [1s ]2 component, that is characterized as a three-body s-
wave resonance built from the s-wave virtual states in the n-n and 8He-n subsystems,
has not been identified in any experiments so far.

Here, we show the energy spectrum and three-body correlations of 10He measured
using the invariant-mass technique with higher statistics and better sensitivities than
previous experiments. It is concluded that the 10He ground state is a three-body s-
wave resonance, where both the n-n and 8He-n subsystems have zero relative angular
momenta. Such a state shows features that arise from the long-range repulsion and
represents an unbound analogue of the universal halo states predicted by Hongo and
Son [10].

---

## Results

The two-neutron unbound 10He was produced through quasi-free knockout (p, 2p)
reaction at 250 MeV/nucleon, using an intense 11Li beam bombarding on the 150-
mm thick liquid hydrogen target of the MINOS device [23]. The 8He fragment and two
neutrons from the 10He decay were detected by the SAMURAI spectrometer [24] and
the neutron detector array NEBULA [25], respectively. The same setup was used in
Refs. [26–30]. Since 8He has no bound excited states, we do not require γ-ray detection
in coincidence.

The three-body relative energy E , which is also the energy of 10He above the
8He + 2n threshold, was reconstructed by the momenta of 8He and the two neutrons.
The typical energy resolution at E = 1 MeV is about σ = 0.15 MeV (see Methods).
To reject the cross-talk background mainly caused by neutron scattering within the
NEBULA detectors, we applied the procedures detailed in Ref. [31] (see Methods).
The overall 2n detection efficiency as a function of E is shown in the upper panel of
Fig. 1, which demonstrates sufficient sensitivity down to the decay threshold.

The lower panel of Fig. 1 shows the relative-energy spectrum after the efficiency
correction, which has much smaller statistical uncertainties compared to two pre-
vious experiments at 61 MeV/nucleon at RIKEN [12] and at 280 MeV/nucleon
at Gesellschaft fu¨r Schwerionenforschung (GSI) [14]. The present spectrum of 10He
shows a low-energy peak at E 1.5 MeV, consistent with the previous results in
Refs [12, 14]. In Refs. [12, 14], the peak at 1.5 MeV has been interpreted as the
ground state of 10He. In addition to this low-energy peak, the current data clearly
show a shoulder structure below 1 MeV, that was unresolved in the spectrum mea-
sured previously at RIKEN but was missing in the GSI result. The difference at small
relative energies has been reported before in the study of 11Li [32] and 6He [33], which
was attributed to the enhanced experimental sensitivity at low relative energies in the
current setup. The low-lying shoulder indicates that the peak at 1.5 MeV is not
the ground state of 10He. Above 2 MeV, the current data, with much better quality,
exhibit strength extending to higher excitation energies.

reaction model. The three-body model reproduces well the ground-state properties of
the 11Li nucleus, including the 2n separation energy, matter and charge radii. The

correlations. The neutron configurations are in reasonable agreement with the recent
results from the 11Li(p, pn) reaction [27]. In the calculation, a 0p -orbital proton

### Reviewer 2

Report on "First identification of a universal three-body s-wave resonance in $^{10}$He"
The subject of this paper is the experimental identification of an Efimov state (resonance) in the $^{10}$He system.
Although Efimov states were first observed in cold atom systems and have long
been discussed in the context of atomic He$_{3}$, they were originally predicted
within the realm of nuclear physics by Efimov. I believe it is extremely
important to identify nuclear systems that can be described by this universal
model, further highlighting the universality of Efimov physics. For this reason,
I think the present paper, especially given its experimental nature, deserves
publication.
I have only a few remarks, which do not pertain to the experimental techniques
that are well explained.
1. A simple remark is on line 6, where the emergence of an infinite tower of
three-body states is related, strictly speaking, to an infinite (and not just a
sufficiently large) scattering length.
2. The explanation of the resonance is mostly based on the shell model
interpretation of the state. It would be useful for a reader from another
community (thanks to the universality of Efimov physics) to at least provide a
sketch of what is happening and why the state appears as a double-intruder
nucleus (lines 45-..., 90-..., and 122).
3. The explanation of the state rests heavily on the shell model. However, there
are other ways to view it that rely on both the scattering length, which has
been extracted (as mentioned again in line 199), and on the effective range
(Kievsky A., Gattobigio M., Girlanda L., Viviani M., *Efimov Physics and
Connections to Nuclear Physics.*, Annu. Rev. Nucl. Part. Sci **71**, 465,
2021). It would be important to try to extract the effective range to allow
for other interpretations of the same state.
4. The grand-angular momentum K is discussed in the Methods section, but I'm not
sure that the introduction of K in line 171 without a previous explanation is
correct.
To summarize, the paper deserves publication as it sheds a nuclear
light on Efimov physics, which originates from Nuclear Physics.

### Reviewer 3

Summary
The manuscript describes measurements of 10He produced through (p, 2p) reactions of a ∼250 MeV/u 11Li beam with a
liquid hydrogen target. Analysis of the three-body relative energy and Jacobi correlation spectra utilized a coupled-channel
three-body model of 11Li combined with the quasi-free knockout reaction model, and complex-scaled solutions of the
Lippmann-Schwinger equation were used to compute final states in 10He. The low-energy structure in the three-body
relative energy spectrum is explained by two 0+ states with 8He cores, one with a [1s1/2]2 neutron component and another
with a [0p1/2]2 neutron component. By tuning the 8He-n interaction to fit the 10He spectrum below 2 MeV, the authors
extracted an s-wave scattering length between 8He and the neutron. The Jacobi-T normalized relative energy and Jacobi-Y
angle 8He-n-n correlations gated on relative energies < 1 MeV show enhancements that are qualitatively reproduced by the
three-body calculations. The authors conclude that the observation of the two 0+ states resolves the long-standing difference
between 10He ground state energies measured from knockout and 2n transfer. Furthermore, the 10He ground state is a
three-body s-wave resonance that exemplifies a novel class of universal three-body bound states.
